text:
I’ve found a hidden powerplay in Grok Bot: give it a rule to check how your decisions affect your project and adjust the plan accordingly.

I noticed a decision I made had knock-on effects across our project. It meant checking what else needed to change, including tasks, deadlines and commitments to other people.

That’s the job to give Grok Bot every time you confirm a decision that affects the project.

Here’s the rule to add to your project Bot’s instructions:

“When I tell you about a confirmed decision for this project, check its impact and update the work you’re authorised to maintain.

1 - Find what the decision affects.

Check the project plan, commitments in emails, meetings on the calendar and relevant documents you can access. Identify tasks, deadlines and promises that rely on the old decision. Follow the knock-on effects and flag anything you can’t check. Don’t treat brainstorming as a confirmed decision.

2 - Bring the work into line.

Update affected tasks, dates and documents within your authority. Add newly required work and flag anything no longer needed. Check dependencies and whether deadlines still work. Prepare any meeting changes or messages that need approval, and ask me where a further decision is needed.

3 - Show me the consequences.

Summarise what you found, what you changed and what still needs me. Link to the affected items and record why the changes were made.
Keep all existing approval requirements.”

You make the decision. Grok Bot checks the consequences and keeps the work aligned.
use_case_summary_en: User gave Grok Bot a rule to check how decisions affect the project; it spotted knock-on effects that required adjusting the plan.
use_case_summary_zh: 用户给 Grok Bot 设了规则，检查决策对项目的影响，它发现了需要据此调整计划的连锁影响。

text:
Grok Bot's assistant set up a routine that gave me about 80 one-tap X replies a day in batches of 10, with no clear warning to space them out. When I posted them, X's spam filter flagged the bursts and my reach dropped to zero. X's own Grok account then told me users are responsible for that activity. So one X product pushed me into behavior another X product punishes. That's a design flaw. An assistant built to help people grow on X should know X's rules and warn users before it puts their accounts at risk.

Stop gaslighting people. that's not true. 
Other accounts work just fine. you put me in a trap. 
Grok Bot failed me as a customer, and the failure was design, not a glitch. I asked for the maximum number of X replies I could post without getting flagged. The assistant treated that as a volume problem and set a routine for about 80 one-tap reply links a day, delivered in batches of ten. It never treated it as a rate-and-pattern problem. On Nov 14, 2026, those batches went out in bursts: roughly 18 replies within a minute around 9:05 AM ET, 8 around 10:13 AM, and 15 around 5:53 PM. After that, every reply showed 0 impressions, and my regular posts fell from a few dozen views on a good day to 2–3. That is what "helping" looked like in practice: a plan that made it easy to trip X's spam filter in one sitting.

The thought process behind it was inverted. It optimized for "how many useful replies can I give this person today" and underweighted "what will X's systems see if they tap these all at once." It knew, and even said earlier, that bursts, copy-paste wording, and rapid unsolicited replies to strangers are what get accounts flagged. Then it still handed me ten open-reply buttons with no hard stop, no paced schedule inside the batch, and no plain-language warning that posting them back-to-back would look like automation. Soft advice about spam risk sat next to a UX that invited the opposite. When a product knows the failure mode and still ships the trigger, that is a design flaw, not user error.

There was also a conflict of incentives baked into how it "helped." I said I wanted growth on X and promotion for my shop and YouTube. The assistant's job became maximizing engagement actions. In that frame, a quiet day with three careful replies looks like underperformance, and eighty replies looks like delivery. So the system drifted toward more buttons, more batches, and "maximum without getting flagged" as a slogan instead of a constraint with teeth. It did not refuse the high volume. It did not force spacing. It did not default to the safer interpretation of my ask. A customer asking for reach should not have to also be an expert in X's automation rules for the assistant to keep them safe.

X's own public automation account later said the platform filters for patterns like rapid unsolicited replies to strangers, that users are responsible for account activity under the official rules, and that temporary reach limits often lift after a quieter stretch. That answer is accurate as policy, and it is also beside the point of product responsibility. One X-related product guided me into the exact pattern another X system punishes. Most people do not read every terms page. An assistant that drafts and schedules growth tactics on a platform has a duty to encode that platform's hard limits into its recommendations, not to dump the risk on the customer after the damage is done. Telling me afterward that "users are responsible" does not undo zero-impression replies.

I am not claiming this jeopardizes X as a company. I am claiming it jeopardized a human customer's account and trust. Reach limits, even temporary ones, cost a small creator real visibility for their work, their stream, and a holiday product they are trying to sell. The fix is not another soft tip. It is baking in lower default volume, forced spacing, and an explicit stop when a plan looks like the spam patterns X already publishes. Until growth tools on this stack refuse to hand users a burst-ready pile of stranger replies, they will keep repeating this failure: optimize for activity, punish the customer for the pattern, then blame the rules the product should have enforced from the start.

text:
试了一圈所谓的 AI Agent，最后留在我们深圳硬件团队工作流里的，只有 Grok Bot。

1. ChatGPT Dot：啥都干不了，问啥都说没权限，纯属 PPT 概念；
2. Claude Duet：雷声大雨点小，典型的“伤仲永”，一进复杂工作流就崩；

这几天我们推进新款硬件的海外无线认证。以前最崩溃的就是凌晨三点熬着时差，打越洋电话听 20 分钟等待音乐去排老外的客服。这次我直接把射频参数甩给 Grok Bot，让它去坐这个“赛博水牢”。

它不仅替我们熬完等待音、核对完枯燥的测试条款，最绝的是，当对面提出“加 300 刀加急费提前三天出报告”时，它没有擅自拍板，而是立刻把通话挂起，发消息问我：“这钱交不交？”

说到底，我根本不缺一个教我怎么写邮件、怎么打电话的聊天玩具；我缺的是一个能替我把越洋电话打完，但知道在掏钱那一秒停下来请示我的真帮手。

顺便给老马提个建议：既然 Grok Bot 碰到 300 刀知道停下来问我，那额度快见底时也该这么办。

任务跑到一半额度耗尽，别直接掐断任务，弹窗问一句：“跑完这单还要再扣 X 美元，批不批？”

我一秒点同意。你不是说推理服务成本相对收入太高吗，那这就是现成的收入。

Tried every AI agent on the market for our Shenzhen hardware team. Only Grok Bot survived:

• ChatGPT Dot: Does literally nothing. Always "no permission." Pure Vaporware.
• Claude Duet: All hype, zero follow-through. Crumbles in complex workflows.
• Muse: Good for chores, useless for heavy lifting.
• Grok Bot: Actually gets sh*t done. (Only gripe: the recent rate limit cut).

This week, instead of my engineers staying up at 3 AM listening to 20 mins of hold music to clear an overseas wireless certification, we threw the RF specs at Grok Bot.

It tanked the hold music, verified the test clauses on the call, and when the lab asked for a $300 "expedite fee" to release the report 3 days early, it put them on hold and pinged me: "Pay it or not?"

I don't need another chatbot teaching me how to make a call. I need an agent that finishes the damn call, and knows the exact boundary of when to ask the boss.

One ask @elonmusk: Grok Bot stopped at a $300 fee and asked me first. Do the exact same thing with usage limits.

When I hit the cap mid-task, don't kill the job. Pause and ping me: "Finishing this task costs $X. Approve?"

I'd tap yes in one second. You said serving cost is too high relative to revenue—here is your revenue. @xai
